title: A new report from Europe raises serious alarms about orbital collisions
gist: The European Space Agency's 2026 Space Environment Report sharply raised its projections for future satellite population and shows collision rates could grow exponentially if current constellation-deployment trends continue, even under best-practice disposal; SpaceX alone now performs nearly 35,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers per month (up from 500/month five years ago) as active satellites have grown from ~1,000 in 2013 to ~17,000 today.

insights.claim: The number of active satellites in orbit has grown from about 1,000 at the time of the film Gravity's 2013 release to approximately 17,000 today, according to CelesTrak.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A 17x increase in active satellites in roughly 12 years quantifies the scale of orbital congestion growth, a key baseline metric for space-sustainability and satellite-insurance risk models.
insights.locator: Today, that number is closer to 17,000, according to CelesTrak

insights.claim: SpaceX's Starlink constellation, with roughly 11,000 satellites currently in orbit and many thousands more planned, is the primary driver of satellite population growth; Amazon has launched hundreds of satellites with thousands more planned, and multiple Chinese Internet constellations are also in progress.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Starlink alone accounts for roughly two-thirds of all active satellites, making SpaceX's operational practices the single most consequential factor in orbital debris/collision risk modeling.
insights.locator: The preponderance of this growth has been driven by SpaceX’s Starlink constellation

insights.claim: A new category of 'orbital data centers' may add hundreds of thousands of additional satellites to orbit, though it remains unclear whether these are economically viable, and ESA's 2026 report projections exclude this category because it consists of projects still being prepared for launch.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: If orbital data centers prove commercially viable, they represent an unmodeled tail risk that could dramatically worsen the collision-rate forecasts already flagged as exponential in ESA's current best-case scenarios.
insights.quote: if they do, they could be the ultimate tipping point for orbital sustainability
insights.locator: Also worth noting: The projections in ESA’s 2026 report

insights.claim: ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report dramatically increased its projections of future satellite population compared to prior years after reassessing the current trajectory of large constellations, citing limited availability of verifiable information on future deployment plans, operational practices, and end-of-life strategies.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A material upward revision by the most credible independent space-debris authority is a signal that prior industry sustainability assumptions were too optimistic, relevant to regulators considering stricter deployment rules.
insights.quote: The notable increase in the index this year is primarily driven by the substantially larger future population resulting from the current extrapolation scenario
insights.locator: There are some striking—and concerning—changes this year

insights.claim: ESA modeling shows that even if satellite operators continue following best practices for disposal and collision avoidance, continued exponential growth in launches leads to an unstable orbital environment with collision rates increasing exponentially by mid-century.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: This is the report's central, most actionable finding: best-practice compliance alone will not prevent runaway collision growth under current launch-rate trajectories, implying policy/regulatory intervention (not just voluntary industry standards) will be needed.
insights.quote: leads to an unstable environment with collision rates increasing exponentially
insights.locator: The extrapolation of our current behavior

insights.claim: A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Donald Kessler found that some orbital bands between roughly 520 km and 1,000 km altitude have already reached a 'collisional-runaway threshold,' meaning serious collisions there could generate new debris faster than gravity naturally removes it.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, already-crossed risk threshold in a defined altitude band (520-1,000 km), giving investors and insurers a concrete zone to monitor for elevated collision/debris risk affecting satellites operating there.
insights.locator: A 2025 paper by Hugh Lewis and Kessler

themes.theme: Contrasting expert views: Kessler syndrome risk

insights.claim: University of Texas at Austin orbital-debris expert Moriba Jah predicts that within the next decade humanity will lose the ability to use certain orbits due to junk saturation, and predicts loss of human life either from school-bus-sized debris surviving reentry and hitting a populated area, or from a civil/commercial astronaut vehicle being struck by unpredicted debris.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A named expert's specific, time-bound (10-year) prediction of fatal debris incidents provides a concrete, trackable forecast for monitoring orbital-risk realization over the coming decade.
insights.quote: I predict that both those things are going to happen in the next decade.
insights.locator: Starting with the pessimists: A few years ago

insights.claim: Elon Musk has publicly downplayed orbital crowding concerns, arguing space is enormous relative to Earth and satellites are comparatively tiny, saying space is not going to get crowded.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Musk's public dismissal of crowding risk, from the operator responsible for the largest share of orbital growth, is a notable divergence from ESA's own exponential-collision-risk modeling and worth weighing against SpaceX's incentive to downplay the risk it is driving.
insights.quote: Space is really big. It’s not like space is gonna get crowded. Space is enormous. If you actually look at it relative to the Earth, the satellites are so tiny you can’t even see them.
insights.locator: during a SpaceX-produced interview this summer

insights.claim: SpaceX's collision-avoidance maneuvers for Starlink jumped from about 500 per month five years ago (on a much smaller constellation) to nearly 35,000 per month as of the most recent reporting period through May 2026 — equivalent to one maneuver every 75 seconds — based on mandatory FCC reporting.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A 70x increase in avoidance maneuvers over five years is a hard operational metric of escalating orbital congestion directly tied to Starlink's own growth, useful for tracking congestion trends via SpaceX's own FCC filings.
insights.quote: That comes to one maneuver every 75 seconds.
insights.locator: We know from mandatory reporting to the Federal Communications Commission

insights.claim: SpaceX uses a far more conservative collision-avoidance trigger threshold than the NASA standard: NASA's standard is a 1-in-10,000 collision probability, while SpaceX started with 1-in-100,000 and has since tightened it further to 3-in-10 million, per a 2025 letter to the FCC.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Explains why SpaceX's maneuver count is so high despite responsible behavior — it is not a sign of near-misses but of an intentionally conservative safety margin, important context for correctly interpreting the maneuver-count metric.
insights.locator: Each maneuver is not a “near miss.”

insights.claim: Spent rocket bodies (upper stages not properly deorbited) are particularly problematic at altitudes of 840 and 975 km, according to LeoLabs space debris expert Darren McKnight, and debris at higher altitudes persists for decades to centuries.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Identifies specific altitude bands (840 km, 975 km) where legacy launch-vehicle debris concentrates, useful for satellite operators and insurers assessing orbital-slot risk.
insights.locator: These school bus-sized stages are particularly problematic

insights.claim: The high density of objects in orbit makes it relatively easy for bad actors to shoot missiles at satellites in low-Earth orbit, creating debris fields that could wipe out communications and cause massive financial damage; the probability of a Kessler-syndrome-type event rises substantially if deliberate anti-satellite attacks occur.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Frames anti-satellite (ASAT) weapons as a geopolitical tail risk that could trigger cascading debris events far faster than organic collision buildup, relevant to defense/space-insurance risk assessments amid rising state actors with satellite capability (e.g., Iran becoming the ninth country with a domestically built satellite).
insights.locator: Finally, because there is so much stuff flying around orbit

insights.claim: No credible experts believe Kessler syndrome could happen imminently from a single collision, but the article's near-term outlook is that operating in orbit will become progressively more expensive due to avoidance technology, personnel, and propellant needs, with launch-window planning around debris becoming more difficult.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Rising orbital operating costs (avoidance tech, propellant, staffing) represent a structural cost headwind for satellite operators that should be factored into long-run unit economics of LEO constellation businesses.
insights.locator: In the near term, it seems unlikely that space will become unusable

insights.claim: The longer-term outlook suggests a Kessler-syndrome-type outcome could become increasingly plausible starting perhaps as early as 15 years from now, though more likely later.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Provides an approximate 15+ year time horizon for elevated Kessler-syndrome plausibility, a useful long-duration risk marker for space-infrastructure investment and insurance underwriting.
insights.quote: Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now but more likely longer
insights.locator: Longer term, perhaps as early as 15 years from now
